catalog_citation: Killian, Don. 2015. Topics in Uduk Phonology and Morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, University of Helsinki. ISBN 978-951-51-1490-7; hdl 10138/156271. 445 pp.
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 Suprasegmental Phonology, §3.1 Introduction p. 40 and §3.2 Tone Inventory pp. 40-41; incidental 'when stressed' remark §2.3.4 Distributional Restrictions p. 25
catalog_quote: Uduk is a tonal language falling into this category. Tone plays a crucial role in Uduk, forming part of the phonology, the syntax, and the morphology. Aspectual grammatical categories are formed by tonal changes in verb roots. There are also irregular modifiers which mark plurality by tone alone, and some person-marking alternations in verbal morphology is also tonal. [...] There are three tone levels, H, M, and L, and four basic tonemes in Uduk: L (à), M (ā), H (á), and LH (ǎ); these exist both on the surface and underlyingly. LM and ML contours do not appear in any lexeme roots. Other contours, such as HL, HM, and MH, occur only rarely, but are possible in both mono- and disyllabic nominal roots. [...] Tone is associated with the syllable in Uduk. As sonorants can be syllabic, they are thus also Tone-Bearing Units (TBUs) in those instances when syllabic. [...] The glottal stop /ʔ/ does not contrast with words beginning with vowels; words beginning with vowels generally insert a glottal stop initially in isolation or when stressed, and otherwise do not use the glottal stop. There is some degree of free variation with this, however.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule stated. The reference grammar treats Uduk word prosody entirely as lexical and grammatical tone (three levels, contour tonemes, TBU = syllable including syllabic sonorants) and never states where word stress falls, whether it is contrastive, or whether it exists at all; the single incidental phrase 'when stressed' (p. 25, about glottal-stop insertion) presupposes some phonetic prominence but gives no placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule given). Tone note: LM and ML contours do not occur in roots; grammatical contour tones trigger phonetic vowel lengthening (p. 40).
new_statements.domain_note: Chali (main) dialect of Uduk, fieldwork 2011-2014; Yabus dialect treated in Appendix B (pp. 305-306) also without any stress statement. Tone described at root/word level; 'leftward realignment' (§3.5) builds phonological words from a lexeme plus following particles.
new_statements.identity_note: Killian 2015 describes the Chali (main) dialect of Uduk (uduk1239); the Yabus dialect is covered only in an appendix. Otero 2019 uses 'Chali Uduk' and 'Yabus Uduk' as the two Uduk varieties. No separate Glottolog dialect codes were checked beyond uduk1239.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Segmental Phonology (pp. 17-38) and Ch. 3 Suprasegmental Phonology (pp. 39-60) describe Uduk as a stable-tone language with three levels (L, M, H) and four basic tonemes, TBU = syllable; no section on stress/accent and no statement of where word stress falls. The word 'stress' occurs only twice in the whole grammar: p. 25 (vowel-initial words 'generally insert a glottal stop initially in isolation or when stressed') and p. 148 fn. 3 (a Siewierska quotation about clitics). Yabus-dialect appendix B (pp. 305-306) likewise silent.

sources.citation: Otero, Manuel Alejandro. 2019. A Historical Reconstruction of the Koman Language Family. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon. hdl 1794/25239.
sources.note: Section 2.1.3 'Overview of Koman tone' (p. 39): all Koman languages have contrastive tone with at least three levels plus rising/falling contours; vowel length not contrastive; TBU = vowel/mora. Zero occurrences of 'stress' or 'accent' in the whole dissertation; Uduk sections (4.5-4.6, pp. 250-252 ff.) treat consonants, vowels and tone only.
